utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. Please sit down. I'd remind you that the affirmation you made to tell the truth still applies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And Mr. Djurdjic is continuing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yesterday we were working with Exhibit P835, so could we please have it on the screens. Could we have item 5 of the English version, or rather, Roman I, subparagraph 5, that's on the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, please take a look at subparagraph 5 of this agreement. Tell us, were you aware of this provision when you arrived at your post?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me then that until the KVM was established, KDOM was supposed to act in place of the verification mission, and then the verification mission would take it over once it was up and running; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I knew about KDOM and its activities was that I was informed that we would at some point absorb the KDOM into KVM, and that was as to the extent of my knowledge with regard to what KDOM's purpose was. I didn't what they did in the field. I didn't know who all their team was, how many they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: That wasn't really what my question was aiming at. All I was asking was that this transition period, so before the KVM was established, the KDOM was supposed to act in their place according to this agreement, and as we know this agreement was signed on the 16th of October, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now have Roman numeral II, that's the next page of the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at subparagraph 1 of Roman II, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, this subparagraph 1 stipulates that your basic task is to actually verify whether there's compliance with Resolution 1199, but this last sentence, "these reports will also be provided to the authorities of the FRY," could you tell me please how did you go about this relating to this particular aspect?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall how those reports found their way to the Government of the FRY, I just don't recall how that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have occasion to see a single report that was sent by KVM to the FRY in the period while you were in Kosovo in the course of 1998 and 1999, and have you had occasion to see it in -- during any of the proceedings where you testified here before this Court?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just don't recall. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that KVM then did not comply with its obligation arising from this subparagraph 1 of item 2 and did not provide reports to the authorities of the FRY?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer that or agree with you on that because I don't know if the mission provided those reports, either some, all, or sporadic reports to the government. I just don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether you reported to OSCE and the Security Council, in other words, the Permanent Council of the OSCE and the Security Council?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of that, we did report noncompliance issues to the Permanent Council, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Who did?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ambassador Walker typically would do that when he would address the Permanent Council periodically verbally, and then there were also reports that were sent down, I believe they went to Mr. Krasnai in the Permanent Council of the OSCE in Vienna.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please scroll up the English version to see item 3 of this agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me, Colonel, that this item, Roman III, provides for the special mandates for the KVM, and under 1 we see that there should be verifications whether cease-fire is being complied with. That is its main function.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we scroll down the English version so we can see the subparagraph 1 of Roman III. From what I can see on the screens right now, the Colonel cannot really see the entire subparagraph. Yes, so this is where it starts and now, please, let's have the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that this is a special mandate, a verification whether there's compliance with cease-fire agreements?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Please now take a look at subparagraph 2. Am I correct, Colonel, that the FRY had the obligation to inform on the movement of its forces in the course of the previous week to inform these KVM headquarters?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was our understanding. That was the intent, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: In other words, this relates to the preceding week, and it is supposed to inform on the movements and where they were. Did you receive these reports on the preceding week movements?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not always, no, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did you seek information from the Vienna Secretariat? Did they receive reports from the FRY authorities relating to the compliance with the agreement which were sent to the Vienna Secretariat?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't speak or have knowledge of what the Secretariat in Vienna received or didn't receive. I don't have any insight on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that the KVM headquarters received daily reports from the MUP -- from the Pristina MUP staff on all events from the previous day?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware that KVM headquarters received some reports. Those reports were not always accurate. For example, can I -- may I elaborate a bit on that, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We would get information that there would be a MUP movement at 9.00, and in fact the movement took place at 6.30. So the timing and the coordination was not always accurate, and we had a terrible time linking our KVM up with the MUP. And the MUP would always give us a reason why they had to depart earlier or later, but it prohibited us from either accompanying them or following them and sometimes we would arrive in the village even after the fact and they'd already departed. So the reporting that you refer to here was not always accurate, and I could also tell you that it was not a regular occurrence, it didn't happen as a matter of routine.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, first of all, Colonel, you're talking about daily reports or daily reporting that is not really stipulated by this agreement in subparagraph 2. What we've seen in this subparagraph 2 is that the reports were supposed to be weekly for the preceding week, but here it says that the director of the verification mission and the staff may be invited to accompany or escort the police within Kosovo. So the headquarters director or head was supposed to ask for this under subparagraph 2 of this agreement.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: But what you've just said a few moments ago, perhaps you received with some delay on the same day that there would be police movements; in other words, much earlier than the week -- dead-line of a week that is provided for by this subparagraph 2. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay, I can agree that there was a delay on receiving the movements of the MUP or even the VJ, but I would tell you that often what we did receive wasn't accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And how did you verify the accuracy of the information provided? Did you verify this by receiving information from some Albanian from the field and then you compared it to the report or did you do it in some other way?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, when we did get the reports from our MUP liaison officer who was working with the MUP, often the KVM mission would go to a village that we were -- had understanding that the MUP was going to visit, and either they didn't arrive or they went to a different village. On occasion, the reports would be accurate and the coordination would be good and the KVM would meet up with the MUP as established, but it was not something that we could rely on in all cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Would you take a look at subparagraph 3 now, please. Would you agree with me that MUP on the basis of subparagraph 3 was entitled to set up check-points, traffic check-points, and check-points in order to prevent crime?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Only if those check-points were set up for some other purpose did they have the responsibility to inform the KVM, or rather, the KVM was entitled to ask for an explanation; is that what this subparagraph provides for?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not write this document. I can assume that that was the intent of that particular paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you now take a look at subparagraph 4.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, sir, am I correct in saying that the verification mission did not have the right to control the activities of the border control units of the FRY in the swath of land 5 kilometres from the border at the time when this agreement was reached under this subparagraph 4?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree that the KVM did not have the authority to control that border area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. But at the request of the verification mission and approval from the border unit, the KVM could also visit those areas; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you agree with me that there were misunderstandings where verifiers wanted to go and verify or actually inspect border units without submitting previous requests to that effect?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were many misunderstandings and complications at the border area for transit of our vehicles, but I'm not sure and I don't recall those misunderstandings, why they resulted, or whether or not the KVM mission that was responsible for that particular job had sent requests to the FRY for access at the border areas. I just don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, sir, perhaps I wasn't clear enough. This paragraph - and all I'm asking about now is the inspections of the border units of Yugoslavia. The verifiers were not allowed to carry out such inspections without having previously submitted a request for these inspections, and frequently it was the case that these verifiers would just show up there without having submitted the prior request and then they were denied this request and this is what actually led to misunderstandings?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no reason to dispute that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please take a look at subparagraph 5 now. Again this has to do with escorts. Am I correct in saying that the verification mission could submit a request to accompany police units in Kosovo as they performed their normal policing roles or at the invitation of the MUP that they could do so?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you ever seen -- did you ever see a request from the verification mission, not necessarily from the headquarters but perhaps also from a coordination centre, so did you ever see a request for accompanying police units as they performed their duties?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw a request, but they typically wouldn't come through my office anyway whether they were formal or informal. We would hear about requests at our staff meeting, that they were submitted, but never saw them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please see the next page of the English version, under Roman IV, subparagraph 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, sir, would you agree with me that this agreement provides for 2.000 unarmed verifiers?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, what is the basis then -- what is the basis for -- for the procurement of weapons for securing the mission, because as a mission, as a verifying mission, you were not actually allowed to be armed. Would you agree with me that such a request was actually a request to alter the terms of this agreement?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that you're misrepresenting what the original request was of the OSCE for weapons. We requested weapons for body-guards for Ambassador Walker, not for the entire mission, so we were talking only about two or three men that would be armed to provide the security for Ambassador Walker. We were not talking about nor we ever requested that the entire mission be armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, sir, I thought you actually read through the entire subparagraph 2. It says: "2.000 unarmed verifiers ..." including the staff "... headquarters and support staff ..." And if the body-guards of Ambassador Walker's are support staff, even they would not be entitled to carrying arms under this subparagraph?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't disagree with that. I will tell you that Ambassador Walker personally asked for personal security based on incidents that we had confronted once we arrived in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I absolutely agree, but I'd like to ask you this: I see that you cooperated or worked together mostly with Mr. Sainovic, Mr. Loncar, and other representatives of the cooperation mission. Do you know whether any steps were taken with the presiding officer of the OSCE or its Secretariat to propose to the FRY government to change or amend the agreement of the 16th of October, so as to enable certain members of the KVM to carry arms?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any knowledge of what the Secretariat did with that information. We requested to them what the need was for the body-guards to be armed for Ambassador Walker. Whether they went through formal channels with the FRY government I don't know. I know that we levied that request to Mr. Sainovic, and he took that request forward to see if he could assist us in meeting that request.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, would you agree that this agreement in its unchanged form remained valid all the way until the 20th of March, 1999, when you left Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Another thing, since I see that this was the topic of much discussion and waste of time, and that is the issue of helicopters. Does this agreement foresee at all that the verification mission have any helicopters?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would just like to put an objection on the record that the commentary about a "waste of time" is inappropriate in the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hannis, but it washes over us. Don't be alarmed. Carry on, please, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question again, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, without the "waste of time" part. Do you agree that the agreement did not foresee for the verification mission to have its own helicopters for medical purposes?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I won't waste any time any further. But while we're still on the topic, although we will go through another two documents for which DZ said they were the Bible of the verification mission, but let's skip ahead for the time being. Do you agree with me that you were completely in the dark as to how to perform the operation of verification based on all the documents we have seen?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't agree with that comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What would be your position in terms of applying the documents we just saw? What was your understanding of them?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those documents are truly a foundation for what the KVM mission would be based on. Once the mission stood up, the requirements for the safety of our people was a top priority for Ambassador Walker. And the reason that we requested the helicopter, a medical helicopter, from the Swiss was purely for evacuating potential KVM members that were wounded. So I look at this as a foundational document that we would on occasion ask assistance with.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. It seems we were speaking at cross-purposes. I may have jumped the gun a bit, but let's go to P387 next and perhaps then I'll rephrase this question and put another one that I had in mind. Colonel, we have a document of the 25th of October, 1998. In the preamble we see the position of the FRY government which was attached to the communique and the military representatives were informed. The basis of this document is actually the communique itself, the press release, hence I'd like to move forward to the next page. Let's have a look at Roman numeral II, sub-items 1, 2, 3, and 4. Colonel, you must have been acquainted with these provisions during your verification mission in Kosovo and Metohija; is that correct? Sorry, I don't mean the data contained therein as such, but the provisions in general.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree with that, that our mission had this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I'm not discussing the information strictly speaking, but simply whether you had any general knowledge of this statement and its items. Were you familiar with it in the course of verification?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall precisely, but I don't have any reason to dispute it. I mean, it wouldn't make -- it would be logical to me that we would be aware of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: This is one of the basic documents for the verification, by virtue of which the FRY government undertook certain obligations to reduce the levels of police units in Kosovo to the level as it was in February 1998; also they obliged that they would not use any calibres larger than 12.7 millimetres; and that the army will withdraw all equipment that was introduced into Kosovo after February. Were you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that I was familiar with it personally. I didn't -- I don't recall this document. I'm sure it was an underpinning and a foundational document for how the mission stood up, but I'm -- I can't give you any specifics about what I knew or didn't know about what I'm reading here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What I read out to you was supposed to be the task of the verification mission, to check whether it was complied with. Let me ask you this: Everything you have been telling us is what you heard from other people because you really did not have a clue what the true task of the verification mission was. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I would disagree with not having a clue of what the mission was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I apologise, I may have been a bit rough, but given the role you had as the Chief of Staff you simply noted down what others heard and said without going into the essence of the matters involved and the -- to the heart of the issue of verification?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: My role, as I previously testified, as the Chief of Staff was initially to set the mission up, and we did that for about six weeks, until we got into the operational aspects of the mission in December. These documents of verification that you have shown me were in the hands of our operational head of mission director, General DZ, and he was responsible for ensuring that the verification was taking place within the boundaries of the documents that were provided. For me to have detailed knowledge of it, I certainly may have in the early part of the mission, but I don't recall all the documents and the scope of the documents that you provided me and how they were applied in the mission. We were aware of the boundaries, we were aware of the mandates, we were aware of the Holbrooke-Milosevic Agreement, we were aware of the 2.000 verifiers, which I would tell you we never did get into Kosovo for a number of reasons. And we were aware that we also had agreements that we could conduct some no-notice inspections, whether that be in barracks, which I think primarily where that was aimed. I can't speak to the border piece of your earlier questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, these documents, as I told you already, were qualified by DZ as being the Bible of the KVM. Given your function - and I accept what you said - but were you involved in the verification mission only as the Chief of Staff of General Walker, who noted down what others said; or did you take active participation, being familiar with the contents of the documents and providing assessments on non -- of non-compliance and whether something was or was not part of the agreement? Can you try and answer that because that will determine what my follow-up questions will be.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Neither myself nor Ambassador Walker acted in the field as true verifiers; that was left to the operations teams and the RC commanders that managed those regions. Our purpose in going into the field was to visit the RC commanders, look at their situations, visit with the people in the villages, observe the activities of the VJ and MUP activities. The verifications were done by the ops teams and they reported back to the RCs and back to the OSCE headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, it seems you misunderstand me. I accept everything you have said so far, but I want to ask you this: A decision as to whether there was a non-compliance or not and a decision to report such non-compliance to certain bodies of this OSCE, that decision was made by Mr. Walker and his associates and all of them had to be acquainted with the provisions of the agreement we have been discussing. I'm asking you this: Did you merely take notes during the meetings, noting down what others heard about the events, or did you actively participate in the decision-making process of whether there was or was not a non-compliance issue? That is why I want to know this because that will determine whether I will continue going through these documents with you or not .

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I took the note --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- I would object. I think this has been asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Carry on, please, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, could you please answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did you only keep records of what others said, noting down their opinions, or did you participate in the making of decisions as to whether something amounted to an instance of non-compliance or not?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not participate in making decisions on issues of non-compliance or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Yesterday on several occasions you said that the Army of Yugoslavia or the MUP violated or were in breach of the agreement. Were you simply conveying what you heard from others during the meetings with Mr. Walker or was that actually your position?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were the positions of Ambassador Walker and General DZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me ask you this: Did you know under what conditions these agreements, the February agreements, came to being?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand your question. What do you mean "conditions"?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have a question. I'm not sure which February agreements we're talking about. Can we refer the witness to a specific document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You could help me as well, Mr. Djurdjic. What February agreements?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It should have been October Agreements rather than February agreements. So what were the conditions in which these October Agreements came into being in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Let's simplify things. Colonel, we have the agreement on verification, then this agreement, and the Milosevic-Byrnes Agreement of the 25th October. Do you know what the situation was in the background of these agreements in terms of the political situation which resulted in all of them being signed?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't participate in the writing of any of those documents, so I don't know what the backgrounds were before I came on board with the mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Were you familiar with the fact that NATO issued an Activation Order to bomb the FRY in October 1998?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall whether I was aware of that or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: During your mandate there, did you know that the decision to bomb was stayed, but that there was always a possibility that in case of non-compliance NATO would re-activate that Activation Order to actually bomb the FRY?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's really beyond the scope of my knowledge of what NATO would do or wouldn't do. We were there to form a mission. The decisions NATO made were clearly out of my hands. I don't know what was happening in the North Atlantic Council with regard to that decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What I'm telling you about did not take place within NATO. It was a fact which existed throughout your mission. All reports and controls of yours --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- were to the effect to the -- to determine whether the agreement was complied with or not --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. -- excuse me, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Djurdjic, you are there in a position of giving evidence, which we've discussed before. You are not putting to the witness whether something was the situation; you are asserting it was and making that, as I understand it, the basis for asking the witness something further. Now, if you want to establish a foundation from the witness, you will need to get him to tell you what that position was and then proceed from there. And he may tell you he didn't know enough about those things to be able to help you, judging from what he said so far.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, why was KDOM supposed to perform its mission to carry out verification until the KVM was set up? Are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of what the political reasons were for why KDOM was to establish its key mission, but my feeling and opinion is is that KDOM was to remain in place until the KVM was operational and functioning on its own, at which time we would absorb the KDOM capability into the KVM mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Although you were not acquainted with the October Agreements in detail, but once you became a member of the KVM did you know that there were dead-lines before which the FRY was supposed to meet the obligations undertaken under the October Agreements?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, I don't -- I just don't recall from memory what, if any, dead-lines were required of us. I knew we had reporting dead-lines. I knew we had -- our ops people were going through verification compliance -- non-compliance documents in detail, learning those. But I do not -- I don't have a memory for what you're asking there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether you're misunderstanding me or not. I'm not talking about your verification mission. I showed you the agreement. Before the KVM was set up and before it became operational, verification issues were supposed to be carried out by the KDOM. Are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar what documents KDOM was operating under, no. I don't know what KDOM's mission was when I got there, and only learned of what it was doing shortly after arrival. What precisely is your question of me?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have P835 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, sir, on page 1, Roman numeral I, sub-item 5, could you please read out loud.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: "KDOM will act in" --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. We've already looked at this paragraph. I don't know why we need him to read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is there something new you need to put from this paragraph, Mr. Djurdjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That seems to be the question I'm putting that the colonel cannot understand. I wanted to jog his memory. I asked him three times and did not receive an answer. The gist of my question is as follows: Was he familiar with this once he assumed his duties, the thing envisaged by sub-para 5, that is to say that KDOM will act in place of the KVM until it is set up. That is the question and I do not seem to be able to receive an answer to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I thought you had the answer more than once and it is crystal clear, that he did not know anything of the details of the functioning and purpose of KDOM until arrival. Shortly after the arrival he learned of the essence of KDOM and that he learnt that it and understood that it would be absorbed into KVM when KVM was fully operational. Is that a summary of what you've said so far?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's his position. You're wanting to ask, I suspect, Mr. Djurdjic: What was the purpose being fulfilled by KDOM which KVM took over, was it the same purpose? I think you're trying to get to why all this verification was occurring, and the problem is this witness may not be the right one. You or your colleague have asked earlier witnesses who may have known more about that, but if I correctly guess what it is that you're aiming toward, that may help you to frame a question or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, am I right in saying that KDOM, until KVM became operational, carried out verification?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have never read the KDOM execution orders on what it was that they were doing. I never travelled with them on any of their visits. I don't know what KDOM actually did. I don't know if they were to assume the same roles that KVM was about to assume. I don't know if they were just observers. I don't know if they were called verifiers. I don't have an answer for you of what the KDOM mission was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. When did the KVM become operational?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to tell you that KVM became operational the day that Ambassador Walker set foot on the ground, which would have been roughly 4 November; however, having said that, we spent four to six weeks just standing up the mission. And we got into the field for the first time in about December of 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this mean that until December 1998 you did not know what was going on in the field?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that KDOM up until -- actually handed over its files up until the take-over by the KVM; and if so, do you know where those files are?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm unaware of documents that KDOM gave to our KVM mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see exhibit -- or rather document D004-4367. Specifically could we see page 23 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, this is your handwriting, I believe, your handwritten notes?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, if we're going to talk about his notes we need to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you going into their content? Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm confused. I have a typed version. Could we see a typewritten version. This should be an entry for the 25th of November. Your Honours, I apologise, are we now in private session? Can I move on? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: So I have in mind the 25th of November, 1998, that entry.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, what was your date there, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: November 25, 1998, a meeting of the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which Executive Board are you referring to, the Permanent Council or ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see page 22 of the English. Ms. O'Leary tells me that this document should be D004-4455, page 22 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, let's try to do it this way because this is a very brief entry that I would like you to comment on. This is an entry of November 25th, 1998. In Serbian it says a meeting of the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is not the right document either. "Italian issues: They're trying to change the nomination. "Call Krasnai - to be in Vienna by Friday. "Where are the Russian representatives?" Is this page 22? Finally we're there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Could you please comment on this final paragraph: "They want Russian in the fusion cell ..."

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I can recall, Mr. K rasnai was kind of the point of contact for us in regard to the Permanent Council on what their concerns and desires were, and one of the issues here was the Russian member state wanted to be sure we had a Russian in the fusion cell. The position of the Permanent Council and later Ambassador Walker was because of the nature of the information that would be in the fusion cell, it might be best that it only be NATO members only in the fusion cell. And that was primarily driven by the reason of having imagery to do the verification. The imagery was sensitive and so there was some reluctance to have a Russian in that cell. I believe that was later resolved and, in fact, we did have Russians in the fusion centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And when was this approximately? Do you recall who it was?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: When was what? The discussion on this? 25 November is the best recollection of date I have based on what's on my notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, I just tagged on to your reply, you said that the Russians later on were in the fusion centre. So my question really was related to that. When did this happen? When were the Russians included in the cell? And do you know the names of the persons who were -- the Russians who were in the fusion cell?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I cannot remember the names of the Russians in the fusion cell. I don't know precisely when they entered the fusion centre. I would -- it would just be a guess if I told you and I would say probably late December time-frame, maybe January. I do not know precisely, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, during the break I will make sure that the numbers of the documents that I call for are organised, in order, so in the meantime I would like to move on to a different topic and then I will return to this later on. I just want to save time, or would you prefer me -- would you prefer us to take the break now so that I can do this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think if you moved on, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Could we then go back to open session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Open.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see D162, Exhibit D162.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, looking at the date here, it would seem to me that you were in the US at this time on leave on the 8th of January, 1999; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember precisely, but I did take leave at some point. So no reason to dispute it, I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, you were for sure, although I see that you don't remember now, but let me try to refresh your memory. I believe you went on leave for New Year's and I believe you returned on the 10th of January, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, I see that you can't recall that, but it doesn't really matter. Just -- I want to ask you this: Are you aware or were you aware of these press releases while you were away from Pristina or maybe did you learn about them later on?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I mean, it -- you know, what I looked at when I was leave, where I went when I was on leave, I didn't have a BlackBerry, so I wasn't getting any reporting. So I would tell you that while I was on the leave I was unaware of press reporting that was coming out of the OSCE, so I would have more than likely learned about them when I came back.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, are you aware of this incident that is reported here in this report?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Do you know that at the same time, maybe even on the same day, there was another patrol that was attacked, a MUP patrol that was attacked in Slivovo, near Stimlje, and that a MUP member was killed?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware that prior to the 15th of January there were a few incidents where MUP police officers were killed or ambushed by KLA, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was Mr. Walker away from Pristina at this time, at the time of this incident, and was he maybe in the US?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe he and I were in the US at the same time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And it seems to me that you spent more time working than having leisure time at this time, do you recall, while you were in Washington?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We made several visits, State Department, Congress, Department of Defence, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me, why did you spend so much time in Washington, DC, on these meetings while Mr. Walker was, in fact, the head of the Kosovo Verification Mission?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you assuming that I was holding these meetings independently of Ambassador Walker?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: No, no. What I said was you were actually accompanying Mr. Walker when he went to attend these meetings, so you were with him at the meetings. And what I'm asking is: Why did Mr. Walker as head of the verification mission, why was he attending all these meetings in the US, in Washington, DC?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay, I understand your question now. Whenever Ambassador Walker went back to Washington, he had to notify the State Department, number one, that he was coming home. And in doing so they put together a schedule for him that they wanted him to execute while he was in Washington. Obviously being an American, being a US ambassador, several people wanted to know what was happening in Kosovo. So he would brief what he knew at the time and answer their questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please see Exhibit D161.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Do you remember this press release?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the incident, but I don't remember the press release.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, and in relation to that incident do you remember that Colonel Ciaglinski was in Decani when this incident occurred, when fire was opened on a KVM patrol on the 15th of January, 1999?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that KVM headquarters, while you were still in the US, issued a press release condemning the KLA because of their attack on a KVM patrol?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would have been a logical event for them to do so. We -- it doesn't surprise me that we issued that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, do you remember that at this time General DZ was actually standing-in for Ambassador Walker and that Mr. Keller was the chief of the staff of the KVM?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that Ambassador Keller ever assumed the Chief of Staff role, but I know that General DZ was assume Ambassador Walker's role in his absence, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, I did not say that he was the Chief of Staff, Mr. Keller, but rather that he stood -- was standing in for Mr. Walker while you were in the United States.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I object. I read his question in the transcript. That is what he said. Maybe there was a translation issue, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It seems to be a translation issue, Mr. Hannis. The issue seems to be whether you are aware, Colonel, of the activity of Ambassador Keller standing in for Ambassador Walker during Ambassador Walker's absence, if I correctly understand where we've got to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So the -- you're asking me did Ambassador Keller ever assume Ambassador Walker's role or did General DZ ever assume that role? I'm a little confused on what your question for me is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, let me try and simplify the question. While you were away from Pristina over the new year holidays, did Mr. Keller stand in for Mr. Walker as the head of the Pristina headquarters?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not a hundred per cent certain, but he did on occasion have Mr. Keller perform that role, as did General DZ also would stand in for Ambassador Walker. I'm not sure at that time which one it was. We typically stayed in touch, when we were away, with General DZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. New, do you remember that Mr. Walker was upset because of the press release of -- by the Kosovo Verification Mission of January 8th, condemning the KLA -- or rather, the press release of the 15th of January, condemning the KLA for the attack on the MUP, on the police, and that there was a phone call where they talked about this being a bit premature. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we need some clarification because the press release we were looking at about the 15th appears to be about KLA attacking or wounding KVM officers. And this question talks about a press release regarding attacks on the MUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Your question seems to have confused two incidents, one on the 8th and one on the 15th of January, Mr. Djurdjic. Which is it that you're asking about, the first press release?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I think I've actually confused these two, and I've ended up with the incident of the 21st, but then I also referred to the press release of the 8th of January. And what I was asking is whether the witness remembered that Mr. Walker was angry because of this condemnation, this denouncement in the press release, and that it was premature because it would actually make the work of the KVM more difficult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: This is a question directed to the press release of the 8th of January concerning the wounding of or killing of three MUP officers and the wounding of two more and civilians.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm -- I do not recall the press report in detail, what that was about. But Ambassador Walker, I know, was upset in regards to the KVM verifiers being shot at. He was upset with each event where there was a MUP policeman injured by the KLA, and I remember him saying on several occasions when he would condemn the KLA for the action that this was not helpful for them, to continue this kind of action.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: All right. I think we will return to this later.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe this is the right time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, how are you going for time, Mr. Djurdjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as I said before, I will comply with that. So whatever time I have left I will try and make my questions a bit briefer and I'm sure that we will complete with this witness questioning today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That I take it is a revised expectation. Last night we were rather given the expectation that you might finish during this first session, so now you see it taking much longer. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we were far more efficient yesterday, and I did not expect that we will take so much time today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is it that you will finish during the next session?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will do my best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We must have our first break now. We will resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please be seated. Yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Could we move into closed session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have D004-4455, page 41. This is not the document. The 29th of November -- yes, this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, could you please comment this entry of yours of the 28th -- sorry, the 29th of November. What was the cause of it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We have on the screen two different documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the English document is the right one. This is what I was looking for. The one in Serbian is not correct, but it is not all that important. We actually want to hear it from the witness. In Serbian it is D004-4504. However, it is irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Could you comment, Colonel, this entry of yours of the 29th of November.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm just waiting for the document. There we go.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please leave the English version now. It is fine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was a note to myself. It was a result of photographs that I had taken on the 27th of November for two Serbian journalists that we had gone out and that were hostages held by the KLA and we had won their release. I took photos of the event. It was really one of the first times that we had gone out into a KLA zone. It was relayed to me that there was an assessment made that I was working for the CIA as some sort of a collections officer. I found it sort of humorous and just made a note of it really for historical purposes. As I mentioned, it's your introduction, I was not a combat air force pilot, but I spent all my years as an intelligence officer in the air force and -- which is why I found what they said to be understanding but it wasn't exactly true.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would ask for D004-4623, please. Page 2, please, in the English version. D004-4623. It should be the 4th of December. In the English page 26. Let's see if the first page is correct. This is fine. Could we next go to page 2, please, that is to say page 27. It mentions the Russian ambassador.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Do you see that? I'm interested in the top entry, and then we'll go back to page 26, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's go to page 26, please, in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: There, Russian ambassador.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you bring it up so I can read it. It's too small a print.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The bottom of the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, "Russian Ambassador continues ..." I'm interested in that part.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe this references Russians in the fusion centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go back to page 27, please, so that you can see the rest of this entry -- but first could we please go to the bottom of page 26 to see whether there was anything else there. Yes, it is the bottom of the page. Okay. Page 27 then.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, what does this mean: "Our lives could be miserable with Russians on the ground"?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was frank conversation between Ambassador Walker and discussions with NATO regarding the Russian contingent that was going to join us. As I recall, there were several demands from the Russians about positions that they wanted. Their issues were time-consuming for the mission. And I recall we had issues with alcohol with the Russians, and I think that those were the kinds of things that we were worried about by having a Russian contingent alongside of us. Secondly, there was a concern with the imagery that we had that would be part of the fusion centre and how we would have to work that with a Russian representative in the fusion centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. This is a conversation with the Secretary-General Mr. Solano on the 4th of December, 1998? Perhaps we should go back to page 26 to see the heading.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please zoom in for the colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Am I right, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this was the discussion we had with Mr. Solano in his office.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At the end of the entry where the Russian ambassador is mentioned it says: "Other confidential information with NATO classification will be forwarded through other channels." That is on page 27 again. The last sub-item at the top of the page, the second one that is.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't speak to that in this environment here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: This has to do with the work of the verification mission, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't know how to treat this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what it is you're asking. What are you wanting?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two things. First, it seems there is some classification of information sent by the KVM only to NATO and through other channels which had nothing to do with the KVM. Which other channels are these and what information did KVM possess that was for NATO only? That was on the 4th of December, 1998. I'm not interested in NATO. I'm interested in the KVM.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you able to throw any light on information gathered by KVM?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The best I could say on the channels was that there was -- this had to do with imagery, so we had a way -- before we went to do a verification on a particular site, we had other evidence that we could look at. The imagery comes from sensitive sources, and that was to be channelled in a different way to the KVM verifiers to look at those sites.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, if I may remind counsel that your order allows Mr. Phillips to decline to answer any questions on the ground of confidentiality where he feels that's necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We have, I think, steered around that, Mr. Hannis, but we will see. Mr. Djurdjic, you've had that answer. Is there any other issue you wish to pursue about this?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm not interested in NATO whatsoever. I'm interested in KVM activities. I want the Chamber to get a full picture of what the actual objectivity of the KVM was. I'm not interested in NATO. What am I interested in? Who made such decisions. Who decided which information was NATO-only and was the Secretariat in Vienna notified of this, that is to say the presiding officer of the OSCE, and whether all OSCE member states were familiarised with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The answer given by the witness suggests this is not information coming from KVM to OSCE, but information provided to KVM to assist them in their function of verification.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in the document it says: "Other sensitive information that is NATO-only." That is to say KVM, not NATO information. Who decided that some KVM information can be NATO-only? It says "NATO-only."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I understand this quite differently from you. Information that has come from NATO that is NATO-only, which they saw as having a security implication if shared with some others, would come a different channel and not through the main KVM.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that's exactly correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then perhaps the translation I have is wrong: [In English] "... that is NATO-only ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Information that is of NATO-only is what I'm reading, not to be shared beyond NATO.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You understand what "imagery" is, do you, Mr. Djurdjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do, but our conclusions seem to differ. In any case, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, what other channels were those?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't speak to those channels because they belong to NATO. It was information that NATO would find a way to get to us. We were not producing NATO-classified or restricted material from KVM.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I'm not interested in the technical aspect. It means that there were some special channels between NATO and the KVM, separate from all others; is that so?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't speak for NATO, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you to. I'm asking you to speak about the KVM. What special channel did you use? Not in the technical sense. Let's skip that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I have document D004-4623, page 36 in English. Page 36, I'm interested in the part that says "KVCC" -- yes, "KVCC" - the coordination centre of the verification mission. "This facility will have all information."

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Was this within the staff, this facility?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Where was the coordination centre of the KVM?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was -- this was in Macedonia, what was referred to as The Shoe Factory. Brigadier-General Montgomery was the initial general officer in charge of that facility and it was a NATO facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to address the Court. If you think I shouldn't or that I'm overstepping the boundaries of what was approved, do let me know and I will move on. If there are any problems, perhaps the Presiding Judge should just caution me and then I will filter my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do understand, Mr. Djurdjic, we know less than you do. We've heard what the witness has said in court. We've heard your questions. We do not know what you are getting at, what you're after, whether that will create a problem or not. So you are ahead of us. At the moment we do not appear to have a problem, but my concern is that you are increasingly straying away from what should be interesting us in this case, what really matters. So if you really see a need to pursue something, we'll hear your questions and if necessary intervene. But it's one thing to see a topic that's interesting because you don't quite know all the answers; it's another thing to see whether that's really going to be important in the hearing of our trial here. I don't see the latter at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, sir, within the verification mission and generally within the OSCE, were special links with NATO approved that would exclude other OSCE member states, such as Russia and maybe some others?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I can say here is we did ask assistance from NATO to provide us a secure link that was honoured. And they gave us a secure telephone, which I had mentioned earlier, and a secure booth to put that telephone in that was accessible only by Ambassador Walker, myself, and General DZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And my question was: Within the OSCE, did you have approval for that? Did you have permission for that from Russia and other states, OSCE states, so that did they approve such links where communications between individuals with NATO were possible?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Permanent Council was aware of it, did approve of the link being established, but that doesn't mean that all the member states agreed with it. I think Russia did object to it, if I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mention that you had access to this, Mr. Walker, and General DZ; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Am I correct in saying that the United States and Great Britain were members of NATO?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please have D004-4623. In the English version that's page 46.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Sir, Colonel, can you see right there under the heading where it says: "Brief - Nick Turnbull ..." Could you read this to yourself up to "forensic brief." Could you tell me, what was the occasion on December 9 for Mr. Nick Turnbull to brief you on Malisevo and provide this information?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was our request to get an understanding of what had happened in Malisevo. It had been a village that had been destroyed and burned and the Albanian inhabitants had left and fled to the mountains, and it was an issue that Ambassador Walker wanted to get a better understanding on what Malisevo was, what it looked like, just a general overview brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But there was a lot of activity by the KVM and Mr. Holbrooke specifically regarding Malisevo in terms of the MUP decreasing their activities, although Malisevo was the centre of this movement. Would you agree with me that a lot of effort was put into reaching some sort of agreement regarding Malisevo?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a tremendous amount of work on Malisevo in terms of bringing back the Albanian population to Malisevo and decreasing the MUP presence in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Doesn't that seem illogical to you, namely, that Malisevo which was the centre of KLA, that one should call for the decreasing of the FRY forces there?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The intent of Malisevo was to make an example of success, which is why Ambassador Holbrooke focused on it so much and asked us to focus on it so much. We had to show in our view, both to the FRY and to the Permanent Member Council, that Malisevo could be KVM's first success story by moving out the MUP, bringing back the Albanians, and then allow us to sort out the KLA. It was on occasion mentioned to us that Malisevo was the KLA capital. Whether it was true or not, I don't have any foundation to make that assessment. That was certainly what was said and what we had heard, but our hope was was to turn it into a success story, both for KVM and for the peace process that we were trying to establish. And our concern was was why there was so many MUP guarding a village that was vacated and burned, and we found no value in that other than being an intimidating factor for the peaceful population to return. I would just like to add, if I may, sir, Mr. Holbrooke had asked me to build a briefing that mapped out a demilitarised zone in Malisevo, and that included both the KLA and the MUP, that we had established a zone, that there were to be absolutely no weapons in that zone. So we had an obligation to make sure that the Albanians who returned were, in fact, peaceful Albanians and not KLA and an obligation to get cooperation from the MUP to decrease their presence and their weapons in the Malisevo. That DMZ concept was taken to Belgrade and briefed to Mr. Milosevic. Ambassador Holbrooke did brief that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, just two matters here. If the village was in such a condition as you state, then there was nowhere for the people to return; and secondly, how could one make an agreement with those who kept engaging in armed conflict and where Malisevo was there centre -- their training centre?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that it was a training centre. I didn't say that. But we definitely needed Albanians to come back to rebuild, and without a population there would be no rebuilding or construction underway there. The city needed to be rebuilt because that was the original home of thousands that had fled. The second reason was as you're talking obviously here December of 1998, which was the winter-time. It was cold and we were certainly worried about the exposure of the Albanian population that fled to the mountains, children, women, that would suffer from such exposure in the mountains. So we needed to get them back. A lot of the village was destroyed. There were some inhabitable structures there, but a lot of work did need to go in to rebuilding it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now have Exhibit -- Prosecution Exhibit P1312, page 30 in English and page 36 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, what I would like to talk about is this entry for January 9, 1999, at 7.45 under item 3 or paragraph 3 I've read and then onwards. Could you take a look at that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 7.34, the entry at 7.34.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Does this help you refresh your memory, these notes here? Do you remember what it was that you noted then what it related to?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe this is related to the Panda Bar in Pec where there were Serbs that were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let me try and help you. You see that this relates to a press statement of January 8th, 1999. At the time you were in the United States and this relates to an attack on the police station in Dulje, and I tried to refresh your memory regarding this event on the basis of that OSCE statement. And now here we can actually see that you've made some notes about this and also what was to be done and there's also mention of Mr. Clark who says: This is an unfortunate press statement made -- could play right into the hands of Belgrade. Bad precedent for future negotiations. This statement is about Suva Reka and you even mention the location there. And then underneath you can see the text that follows. I don't to read it out loud. And at this time Mr. DZ and Keller were in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, is there a question? And if so, it certainly seems to be compound.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We've had a summary with some liberties of what is here. Now, Mr. Djurdjic, what is it that you would like the witness to assist you with about this? Are you asking him does he now remember?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I wish to refresh his memory because here we see that these are notes of a conversation between Mr. Walker and Mr. Clark in Pristina about this statement because Mr. Walker was unhappy with the content of this statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... no need to go over it again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I might be able to help here. There is a word here that I know is a sensitive issue, but I would have to look at the original press release. If I recall this now the line here that says: "I read the 8 January press statement calling the KLA terrorists ..." That was a major issue for KVM because it was a mandate of Ambassador Walker, Your Honour, not to refer to the KLA as terrorists. Belgrade referred to them as terrorists and the Russians referred to them as terrorists, but we were not making a judgement on who or what they were. And I think that was the exception of the press release that Ambassador Keller, French deputy, released, and that's what upset Ambassador Walker, and that created problems for NATO because now we're talking a terrorist faction. And it's in the KVM press line which means that we have identified them as terrorists, and that was never our position. I think that is the key piece of this line of questioning that I'm being asked here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see page 31, or rather, 32 in English and page 39 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: The excerpt that you will see is an entry for January 10th, 1999, and it's your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see page 32. It's the same document, P1312.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That is page 32 of 1312, Your Honour. If counsel could tell me what he's looking for I might be able to assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Hannis, in the B/C/S version I see Walker spoke with Wes Clark, very concerned, that's what I have in B/C/S but I don't see that -- the corresponding text in English. Well, let's try page 31.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That English is at the bottom of e-court page 31 in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do you have a specific question, Mr. Djurdjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, you see here you stated that Mr. Walker was worried because the KLA is to blame, because this undercuts NATO authority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: The question is: Why is Mr. Walker worried if the -- if the KLA actually breached the agreement and how does this undercut NATO?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The note speaks of "the press is playing this as KLA is to blame ..." rather than it being the fact, it's the way it is being presented in the media, which seems to be the point of this note. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have an objection because I think the question is vague and assumes something that has been established yet about who is worried between the two speakers that are mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Fair comment. Yes, Mr. Djurdjic, you are assuming one of the two people is the worried person. It may be the other one. But if we get past that, you can then be concerned about what I was saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm asking for clarification from the Colonel, so perhaps -- well, we see what is written down here, but maybe he can tell us what it was that he wrote down and why.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me try to give you a comment here. I don't remember this piece exactly, but I do know one of the worries at this time was the escalation of events on both sides, the KLA and the MUP, that would create an excuse for larger MUP and VJ presence which would continue to escalate the problems that we were trying to de-escalate. The KLA was not helpful in any of this. And whether -- I think the comment there about the KLA to blame because it undercuts NATO, we wanted a peaceful process, obviously. And with the KLA acting we were worried that, as I mentioned, the VJ would step up and then there would possibly be NATO action which was something that worried both sides. So that's about the best I can do to explain that. I don't remember it completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And this portion where it says: "French are playing this to their own advantage ..." What is that supposed to mean?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the French were very pro-Serbian, and we were trying to keep a very unbiassed reporting and an unbiassed capacity in our mission. And Ambassador Walker felt that this was highlighting the Serbian opportunity for increased deployments. The bottom line there was Ambassador Walker didn't feel this was very unbiassed reporting.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And this is something that he discussed with Mr. Clark, but did he discuss this perhaps later on with Mr. Keller and other deputies or other assistants?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: He discussed this -- I believe our press lead at the time was a French woman, her first name was Beatrice. He did discuss this with Ambassador Keller, and I do remember it being a very heated discussion. It was not a pleasant period, and I recall Ambassador Walker saying that he should have seen that press release and approved it before it had gone out even though he was in the United States.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see page 34 in English, at the very bottom of the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, the P there, what does that stand for? Is that -- does that stand for Mr. Pickering I assume?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that was Mr. Pickering's comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, what is confusing here, we also see H, W, P, and R, whereas it says that there were three participants there, Pickering, Walker, and Phillips.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
